notes.meaning: King David promised Shimei with an oath that he would not be put to death. Because David had just received mercy from God, he chose to forgive a man who had cursed him. Those who have experienced God's kindness should be quick to show mercy to others.

Mephibosheth, the grandson of King Saul, came down to meet David. He had neglected his feet, left his mustache untrimmed, and worn unwashed clothes ever since David fled. These were clear signs of deep personal sorrow over the king's troubles.

When Mephibosheth arrived to greet David, the king asked why he had not gone into exile with him. David asked this because Ziba had previously claimed Mephibosheth stayed behind to seize the throne. This gave Mephibosheth an opportunity to explain what had truly happened.

Mephibosheth answered that his servant Ziba had deceived him. Being lame in both feet, Mephibosheth planned to have his donkey saddled so he could ride along with the king. Instead, Ziba took off on his own and left his master stranded.

Mephibosheth explained that Ziba had told wicked lies about him to David. Even so, he praised the king as wise like an angel of God who could see through falsehood. He humbly left the entire matter in David's hands to decide what was best.

Mephibosheth noted that his whole family had been at the mercy of David and deserved nothing from him. Yet David had graciously treated him like family by giving him a seat at the king's table. Because he had already received such undeserved kindness, he felt he had no right to make demands.

David told Mephibosheth to stop speaking of the matter and ordered the land to be divided between him and Ziba. This ruling restored the earlier arrangement where Mephibosheth was the owner and Ziba farmed the estate for him. David chose to settle the dispute swiftly without punishing Ziba for his slander.

Mephibosheth told David that Ziba could keep all the property for himself. His only real concern was that the king had returned safely to his home in peace. His unselfish words showed that honoring his king mattered far more to him than holding land.
Barzillai, an older leader from Gilead, came down from Rogelim to escort David across the Jordan River. He made the journey to show honor to his rightful king and see him safely on his way.

Barzillai was eighty years old and very wealthy. When David fled in distress and stayed at Mahanaim, Barzillai used his wealth to feed and supply the king's camp. He generously shared what God had given him to care for the Lord's servant.

David invited Barzillai to cross the Jordan and live beside him in Jerusalem. The king wanted to reward Barzillai by providing for him at court and enjoying his wise friendship. David showed genuine thankfulness to a man who had stood by him during his darkest days.

Barzillai asked how many years he had left to live that he should relocate to the capital city. He knew he was too old to start a busy life in royal service. It was time for him to prepare for death rather than seek position at court.

Barzillai explained that at eighty years of age, his senses had grown dull. He could no longer enjoy the taste of delicious foods or take delight in the singing of court musicians. He did not want to become an extra burden to the king in his old age.

Barzillai stated that he could only accompany the king a short distance past the Jordan River. He asked why the king would offer him such a lavish reward for simply doing what was right. He had supported David out of loyalty rather than a desire for personal gain.

Barzillai asked permission to return home so he could die in his own town near his parents' tomb. He offered his son Chimham to cross over with the king instead, asking David to show kindness to the young man. He preferred to help the next generation step forward while he quietly prepared for death.

David agreed to bring Chimham with him and promised to treat him with great favor. He also told Barzillai that he would gladly grant whatever request the older man asked of him. David gladly used his royal influence to honor and care for a loyal friend.

After all the people had crossed the Jordan, King David crossed over as well. The king gave Barzillai an affectionate kiss and a parting blessing of peace, and Barzillai returned home. David showed deep gratitude to a faithful friend before they went their separate ways.

David traveled forward to Gilgal with Chimham alongside him. All the men of Judah and half the men of Israel came together to escort the king. This company showed that people from across the nation were gathering to welcome David back to his throne.

The leaders of the northern tribes of Israel came to David with an angry complaint. They asked why their brothers from Judah had brought the king across the Jordan in secret without including them. They felt pushed aside and suspected Judah was trying to claim all the king's favor.

The men of Judah answered that they took the lead because David was their close tribal relative. They denied seeking any personal gain, explaining that they had paid their own expenses and received no royal gifts. They defended their quick action as an act of pure family devotion.

The northern tribes answered that they made up ten tribes and therefore held a larger share in the king than Judah did. They argued that they had spoken first about restoring David, so Judah had treated them with disrespect. However, the men of Judah replied with even harsher words, stirring up bitter division between the tribes.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some Catholic commentators note that the population gap between Israel and Judah was not truly ten to one, making Israel's boast of higher honor unfounded.
